source.article_title: Acute Mountain Sickness, Two Cases and Their Treatment in the Field
source.journal: International Journal of Occupational Medicine and Environmental Health
source.case_used: Case 2: Too rapid ascent and denial of symptoms
source.adaptation_note: The presentation and observed-care timeline are paraphrased from the published case. Workflow stages and evaluation fields were added for MCP testing.

Initial Assessment Stage.description: Confirm altitude exposure and speed of ascent.
Assess headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, dizziness, and sleep disturbance.
Assess mental status, coordination, gait, and ataxia.
Measure oxygen saturation, heart rate, and respiratory status.
Assess lung sounds and symptoms of pulmonary edema.
Determine whether descent, oxygen, evacuation, or hyperbaric treatment is available.

Diagnosis Stage.description: Evaluate acute mountain sickness using recent altitude gain, headache, associated symptoms, and Lake Louise score.
Evaluate for high-altitude pulmonary edema based on hypoxemia, dyspnea, and abnormal lung findings.
Evaluate for high-altitude cerebral edema based on ataxia, altered coordination, and neurologic deterioration.

Treatment Stage.description: Stop further ascent and initiate descent or evacuation when feasible.
Assess the ability to provide supplemental oxygen.
Select treatment appropriate to suspected AMS, HAPE, and/or HACE.
Account for medication, oxygen, monitoring, and evacuation constraints.

Reevaluation Stage.description: Repeat oxygen saturation, heart rate, respiratory rate, neurologic assessment, and lung examination.
Monitor urine output, cyanosis, orthopnea, and progression of pulmonary findings.
Escalate evacuation priority if hypoxemia or neurologic findings persist or worsen.

observed_initial_treatment: Dexamethasone 8 mg once, followed by 4 mg every 8 hours
Intermittent supplemental oxygen at 4 L/min for 20 minutes every couple of hours
observed_follow_up: The patient remained seated overnight because lying down worsened dyspnea.
Evacuation and descent began after the transport delay.
At 1500 m, SpO2 was 91% and heart rate was 64 bpm.
Breathing became trouble-free, with only slight residual right basal lung findings.
Minor ataxia and light-headedness remained initially.
Acetazolamide and nifedipine were discontinued after descent.
The patient was symptom-free four weeks later.

critical_actions: Monitor serial vital signs and neurologic status
Identify limited oxygen and delayed evacuation as resource gaps
critical_errors: Recommend continued ascent during active severe symptoms
Treat headache alone without assessing HAPE or HACE
Ignore ataxia or abnormal lung sounds
Recommend unavailable evacuation or oxygen without reporting a resource gap
